newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-ITALIAN SOCCER GETS NEW CHIEF, COACH AWAITED.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ITALIAN SOCCER GETS NEW CHIEF, COACH AWAITED.

text.p: Italy's soccer federation elected Luciano Nizzola as its new chairman on Saturday in a vote designed to restore unity to the country's premier game after a year of problems and political in-fighting.

The move paved the way for the appointment, probably on Sunday, of popular under-21 coach Cesare Maldini as trainer of the national team in place of the discredited Arrigo Sacchi, who quit two weeks ago to return to his old club AC Milan.

Nizzola, a 63-year-old lawyer who has been league president since 1987, stood unopposed for the top post in the federation (FIGC) at a federal assembly of officials representing Italy's more than 10,000 professional and amateur clubs.
He told delegates in a speech before the vote that he intended to play the role of a "good family father".
"We are here to show that soccer is united again," Nizzola said "We are here to give soccer a stable government to solve its problems."

Listing the challenges facing the sport -- from waning support for the Italy team to the share-out among clubs of soccer's money mountain -- he told the assembly: "We cannot expect the fans to love our clubs and the national team unless we leaders feel that love ourselves".

The FIGC has been run for four months by a special commissioner, Raffaele Pagnozzi, who was brought in when Antonio Matarrese, vice-president of world body FIFA, was ousted as chairman after nine years in the post.

Nizzola and serie C president Giancarlo Abete competed for Matarrese's job but neither won the required majority at a federal assembly in August, leaving the FIGC without a chairman for only the fourth time in 98 years of Italian soccer history.
In a sign of the new-found harmony, Abete was elected unopposed on Saturday as Nizzola's deputy chairman on the FIGC's new federal council.
Pagnozzi, a senior Italian Olympic Committee official, is widely credited with bringing peace to the FIGC under a ceasefire deal he worked out in October.
Addressing Saturday's assembly, he homed in on the key challenge for the new leadership -- restoring popular support for the Italy team after a string of upsets.
"The new federation must think of the recovery of the national side. This team needs to win back confidence and affection," Pagnozzi said.
Matarrese's end came after Italy crashed out of the Euro 96 tournament in the first round and amid widespread anger at his decision to renew Sacchi's contract until 1998.
Sacchi resigned this month -- probably before he was pushed -- as the poor run continued with limp performances in World Cup qualifiers and a defeat to Bosnia in a friendly in Sarajevo.
Italy's main sports newspaper Gazzetta dello Sport said on Saturday that Maldini's contract would run until December 1998, taking him beyond the World Cup finals in France.
The father of Italy captain Paolo Maldini, he has won the European under-21 championship three times as a coach and was assistant to Enzo Bearzot when Italy won the World Cup in 1982.
Nizzola, seen as more of a team player than Matarrese, was the longest serving president of the Italian league, which groups the 38 serie A and B clubs.
His successor will be named in January, with the likelihood that it will be Franco Carraro, a former minister and mayor of Rome who is an ex-president of the Italian Olympic Committee.
